A helper is a value the plant's people own rather than a PLC. "Line 2 is in
changeover." "Today's batch target is 1,250 kg." "B shift is on." "Twelve
parts scrapped since the last reset." "The purge has nine minutes left." None of
that lives in a register, and all of it is exactly what rules and screens need
to know.

HotLoop has seven kinds of them. A helper is an entity like any other: it
has an `entity_id`, a state, attributes and services, it sits on the
equipment tree, it shows up in `/api/states`, on the Entities screen, in `list_entities` over MCP, and in an
automation's state trigger. What is different is where its value lives:
HotLoop keeps it, in the database, and **no service of a helper ever writes a
tag**.

## The seven

| Domain | State | Options | Services |
|---|---|---|---|
| `input_boolean` | `on` / `off` | `initial` (true/false), `restore` | `turn_on`, `turn_off`, `toggle` |
| `input_number` | the number, `"1250"` | `min`, `max` (both required), `step` (default 1), `mode` (`slider` or `box`), `initial`, `restore`, and a `unit_of_measurement` | `set_value {value}`, `increment`, `decrement` |
| `input_select` | the choice | `choices` (required, up to 100), `initial`, `restore` | `select_option {option}`, `select_next {cycle}`, `select_previous {cycle}` |
| `input_text` | the text | `max_length` (default and ceiling 255), `pattern`, `initial`, `restore` | `set_value {value}` |
| `input_counter` | a whole number | `initial` (default 0), `step` (default 1), `min`, `max`, `restore` | `increment`, `decrement`, `reset`, `set_value {value}` |
| `timer` | `idle` / `active` / `paused` | `duration_sec` (required, 1 second to 7 days), `restore` | `start {duration}`, `pause`, `cancel`, `finish` |
| `schedule` | `on` / `off` | `schedule` (required) | none: it follows the clock |

The counter is `input_counter`, not `counter`. `counter` is already the PLC
composite whose reset writes a tag, and it stays exactly what it is.

Every option is checked when the helper is saved, and `initial` against all
the others: an `input_number` from 0 to 100 that starts at 150 is refused, not
started at 100. An option a domain does not take is an error, not a setting
quietly ignored. The helper options (`initial`, `restore`, `choices`,
`duration_sec`, `mode`, `schedule`) are refused on every other domain for the
same reason.

## Making one

An admin makes helpers (`entities.write`). On the Entities screen, **New
helper**, next to New equipment. Over the API:

```
POST /api/helpers
{"name": "Batch target", "domain": "input_number", "unit_of_measurement": "kg",
 "options": {"min": 0, "max": 5000, "step": 50, "initial": 1000}}
```

The `entity_id` is made from the name (`input_number.batch_target`) unless you
give one. `PUT /api/helpers/{entity_id}` changes its name, icon, unit or
options; `DELETE /api/helpers/{entity_id}` deletes it and its value. The whole
API is in [API.md](/iot/api/#helpers).

A change of options that would leave the helper's current value outside them is
refused: narrowing a range past the value, or removing the choice that is
selected. Set the value first, or choose options that include it. A value is
never moved to fit.

## Setting one

Anybody with `helpers.write` sets helpers. Operators hold it: running the shift
selector and counting scrap is operation, not configuration. Viewers do not.
It is not `values.write`, because a helper writes no tag.

Setting a helper is an entity service call, the same call every other entity
takes:

```
POST /api/services/input_counter/increment   {"entity_id": "input_counter.scrap", "reason": "short shot"}
POST /api/services/timer/start               {"entity_id": "timer.purge", "duration": "0:15:00"}
```

The answer says what the helper is now: `{"call_id": "...", "state": "13",
"writes": []}`. `?dry_run=true` works too and answers in the same words the
real call would, without changing anything.

On the Entities screen a helper gets its own tile, never folded into another
(it has no tags to fold by), with its controls for whoever holds
`helpers.write`. Every change is confirmed first, with a reason, like every
other command.

From MCP there is no new tool: `list_entities` finds helpers, `get_states`
reads them, `call_service` sets them. An agent changes a helper only on a
deployment with `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES` and `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_MCP_WRITES` both on,
the same switches a write to a tag needs. A helper moves no equipment, but it
is what rules act on, and an agent flipping the changeover switch is an agent
starting whatever the changeover rule does.

## Refused, never clamped

A value a helper will not take is refused, and nothing changes:

- a number outside `min`..`max`, or off its `step` (counted from `min`);
- an `increment` that would pass `max`, a `decrement` that would pass `min`
  (refused, not stopped at the limit: "stopped at the limit" is a value
  nobody asked for);
- an option that is not one of the choices; `select_next` past the last choice
  with `cycle: false`;
- a text longer than `max_length`, or not matching `pattern` (the whole text
  must match);
- a count that is not a whole number, or past the counter's `min` or `max`;
- a timer paused when it is not running, cancelled or finished when it is idle,
  or started for less than a second or more than seven days;
- a disabled helper; a caller without `helpers.write`; an agent with MCP writes
  off.

Every refusal is a warning in the system log (`GET /api/events`) against the
helper, with who asked and why it was refused, exactly like a refused alarm
acknowledgement. A mistake in the request itself (a field the service does not
take, `"50"` where a number goes) is the caller's error, answered 400, and
changes and records nothing.

## Where changes are recorded

Every change is one line in the system log against the helper: who, from what,
to what, the call id, where it came from, and the reason if one was given.

```
otto   input_counter.increment: 12 -> 13; reason: short shot
system timer finished: active -> idle, due at 2026-09-27T21:10:00Z
```

The line is written in the same transaction as the value, so there is never a
change without its line or a line without its change.

A change of state is also a line in the [logbook](/iot/logbook/), in that same
transaction, with the same who, source and call id. It is written by the
process that made the change, whichever one that is, so an agent's change
through `--mcp-stdio` is logged too, and logged once. Helper lines are never
rate-limited: every one is somebody deciding something. A call that leaves the
state as it was (a number set to the value it already has) is in the system
log but not the logbook, because nothing changed.

## Restarts

A helper keeps its value across a restart: the Gateway comes back with the
shift still B and the counter still 13. Set `restore: false` on one that should
start fresh every time (a "since the last restart" counter): the Gateway puts it
back to its initial value as it starts, and says so in the log. Only the
Gateway itself does that. An `--mcp-stdio` process an agent starts beside a
running Gateway holds the same helpers and hears every change, but never resets
anything, because resetting the plant's values because an agent connected
would be absurd.

## Timers

A timer runs on the wall clock. Started for ten minutes, it finishes ten
minutes later whatever happens in between: a restart that took two minutes
leaves it eight to run. A paused timer stays paused, with the time it had left,
across any number of restarts, and `start` resumes it.

A timer that ran out **while no HotLoop was running** is put back to `idle`
when HotLoop next starts, with `finished_late_at` set to when it was due, and a
warning in the log. **Nothing fires for it.** A rule waiting for that timer to
go idle does not run, because the engine's first look at it after a start is a
baseline, not a change. Whatever it was timing (a purge, a cure) happened long
ago or not at all, and doing it now, late and unasked, is worse than saying it
was missed. Look for `finished_late_at` and decide.

A timer is not an interlock. It runs on a process's clock, through a database
and a network, to the second and usually the millisecond. Anything that must
stop on time belongs in the PLC.

## Schedules

A schedule is on inside its blocks and off outside them:

```json
{"schedule": {
  "mon": [{"from": "06:00", "to": "14:00", "data": {"crew": "A"}},
          {"from": "14:00", "to": "22:00", "data": {"crew": "B"}}],
  "fri": [{"from": "22:00", "to": "06:00", "data": {"crew": "C"}}]
}}
```

- The days are `mon` to `sun`. A time is `HH:MM` or `HH:MM:SS`; `24:00` is the
  end of a day.
- A block whose `to` is earlier than its `from` runs past midnight: Friday's
  22:00 to 06:00 is on until Saturday 06:00.
- Blocks that touch are one stretch of on; blocks that overlap are refused,
  because which one's data applies would be a guess.
- While a block is on, its `data` is in the entity's attributes (`crew: "B"`),
  and `next_event` always says when the schedule next changes.
- It is read on the wall clock in the site's timezone
  (`HOTLOOP_SITE_TIMEZONE`), because a shift that starts at 06:00 starts at
  06:00 on the day the clocks change too. On the night the clocks go forward,
  the hour that does not happen is not on; on the night they go back, the hour
  that happens twice is on both times.

## More than one process

Every change is announced with Postgres `NOTIFY`, and every process holding the
helpers listens. A helper set in one process shows its new value in every
other within a round trip, a helper created or deleted in one appears or goes
in the others, and a change made through `PUT /api/helpers/{entity_id}` is
picked up the same way (one made through `PUT /api/entities/{entity_id}`
reaches the others on their next registry sync, as any entity's does). Every write
is conditional on the row's revision, so two processes counting the same
counter at once never lose a count, and a timer both hold is finished by exactly
one of them.

## Backups

Helpers are in every backup: their configuration with the entities, and their
values in `helper_state`, revisions included. A restored plant comes back with
the shift, the targets and the counts it had, and a timer that was running is
still running on the wall clock (or, if it ran out in the meantime, idle and
marked late, as above).

## In automations

A helper is what rules act on and set:

```json
{"triggers": [{"type": "state", "entityId": "input_boolean.changeover", "to": "on"}],
 "actions": [{"type": "call_service", "params": {"entityId": "number.line_2_speed_sp",
   "service": "number.set_value", "data": {"value": 0}}}]}
```

The rule's write to the tag goes through the write gate like any other, with
the rule as the actor. `states['input_select.shift'] == 'B'` works in a
condition, and a rule can set a helper with `call_service` the same way it sets
a switch.
